extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards governing what rights pass to purchasers or vendees when patented articles, their materials, or machines are sold — including implied licenses, limits on repair vs reconstruction, territorial/time/method/quantity limits, and effects of later events (assignments, judgments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purchase of materials/elements does not convey right to make or use combination (general rule) with one exception
rubrics_metrics.description: A purchaser of the materials of which an article consists, or of the elements of which it is combined, obtains thereby no right to make and use the article, or to unite the elements and employ them in the combination, although the vendor is the owner of the patent in which the combination or the article is claimed. To this rule there is one exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception stated immediately after: "The sale of any object which can be used only in constructing a patented article, or in practising a patented art, is presumed to have been intended both by the buyer and seller for that specific use; and when the seller is the owner of the patent for the article or art, his act of sale confers a license on the purchaser to employ the object for that purpose." (text cites cases and explains the presumption).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale of complete article by patentee carries license to use its materials/elements as united
rubrics_metrics.description: The sale of the complete article by one who owns a patent for the materials of which it is composed, or of a combination by the patentee of its essential elements, carries a license to employ the materials in the article, or the elements in combination, and to use them, thus united or combined, without restriction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained with cases (e.g., Adams v. Burke, Goodyear v. Beverly Rubber Co.). The treatise emphasizes that when patentee or assignee with full right sells a machine/article, he 'parts with' his exclusive right in that specific article so far as its use while it exists. See cited authorities (Adams v. Burke, Mitchell v. Hawley, Blanchard v. Whitney).

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied license includes right to use, repair, and sell; right to use unlimited in duration, place, method, and quantity
rubrics_metrics.description: This implied license of the purchaser and his vendees includes the right to use and the right to repair and the right to sell. His right to use is unlimited in duration. ... It is likewise unlimited in method. ... It is, finally, unlimited in quantity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explains that the purchaser's rights (use/repair/sell) persist through patent expiration and renewal/extension (even by special act of Congress) and generally worldwide use, subject to narrow exceptions (e.g., explicit restrictions by the seller or certain territorial licenses). Cases: Adams v. Burke; Mitchell v. Hawley; Blanchard v. Whitney; others cited supporting place/duration/method/quantity breadth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to use continues during patent term and during statutory or special extensions
rubrics_metrics.description: The right to use the article so long as it was capable of use continues not only during the original term of the patent ... but unlike the right under an express license it subsists during an extension, even though such extension be conferred by special act of Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treatise cites multiple cases holding that a purchaser's right to use survives patent renewals/extensions (e.g., Adams v. Burke; Hawley v. Mitchell; Bloomer v. McQuewan). There are nuances where a sale or license expressly limits duration/place which can bind vendees if known/recorded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to repair does not include right to make or to reconstruct as matter of traffic
rubrics_metrics.description: The right of the purchaser to repair the article does not embrace the right to make a new one nor to reconstruct the old. He may replace its worn-out parts or elements with others, even when these are of the essence of the invention. But when its original materials disappear, the article which he purchased ceases to exist, and with it the implied license to repair and use it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes repair (permitted) from reconstruction (not permitted). Examples and cases: Mitchell v. Hawley, Union Metallic Cartridge Co. v. United States Cartridge Co., American Cotton Tie Co. v. Simmons (where rebuilding that destroys identity attaches no implied license). The treatise analyzes whether replacement or repair preserves identity of the original article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial repairs and replacement of essential parts are allowed if identity of the machine remains
rubrics_metrics.description: Repairing partial injuries, whether they occur from accident or from wear and tear, is only refitting a machine for use. ... It is no more than the exercise of that right of care which every one may use to give duration to that which he owns. When the wearing or injury is partial then repair is restoration, or and not reconstruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court examples show purchasers may replace even essential parts as long as the machine's identity remains (Gottfried v. Conrad Seipp Brewing Co.; Farrington v. Water Commissioners of Detroit; Wilson v. Simpson). The boundary question (when repair becomes reconstruction that destroys identity) is fact-specific and often decided on the evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale including patented consumable components may license their use until exhausted but not replacement
rubrics_metrics.description: That the sale of a machine, in which needles covered by a different patent of the same patentee are used, carries a license to use those needles until they are used up, but not to replace them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific example cited (Aiken v. Manchester Flint Works). The treatise distinguishes consumables embedded in sold machines: purchaser may use consumables as part of the sold article but replacement/re-manufacture of those patented components may constitute infringement if covered by separate patent rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purchaser runs risk of vendor's right to sell, but is not bound by vendor's unknown prior covenants or later conveyances
rubrics_metrics.description: The purchaser of a patented article runs his own risk of his vendor's right to sell. But, if his vendor has received this right, the vendee is not bound by any previous covenants between the vendor and third parties of which he has no notice at the time of sale, nor can he be affected by any subsequent conveyance of the vendor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise explains that bona fide purchasers who buy from someone who has apparent right to sell take free of secret prior covenants the purchaser does not know. Authorities: Metropolitan Washing Machine Co. v. Earle; Bloomer v. McQuewan; discussion on limits where vendor's right is genuinely limited and apparent to purchaser.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of territorial licenses and sales: purchaser's use vs resale rights
rubrics_metrics.description: That the purchaser of a patented article from a grantee may use it anywhere, and the sale is lawful though the grantee knows that it will be used outside his territory. ... That the purchaser of patented articles from a territorial grantee has no implied license to sell them outside such territory, as a matter of trade, though he may use them anywhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise collects authorities (Hobbie v. Smith; Adams v. Burke; McKay v. Wooster; Hatch v. Adams; Hatch v. Hall) and notes nuances: (1) purchasers may often use articles outside the grantee's territory; (2) a license limiting sales to a territory can bind vendees if those limits are express and known; (3) licensees may sell within territory to persons who will use outside, but cannot themselves export as a matter of trade where restricted — facts and contract terms control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vendor who lacked right at sale but later acquires interest is estopped from denying purchaser's right
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a vendor, having no right to sell the patented article at the time of the purchase, afterwards acquires an interest in the patent by which a present right to sell is vested in him, ... the title of the former purchaser to the patented article becomes valid by estoppel, and from thenceforward his right to use it is complete against his vendor, and all subsequent vendees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited case law: Gottfried v. Miller and others. The treatise frames this as an implied license produced by estoppel when the vendor later acquires the necessary patent interest or assigns the territorial right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satisfaction of patentee's judgment or recovery of profits can validate purchasers' rights (payment as substitute for license fees)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the owner of the patent receives his compensation by license-fees or royalties, or makes and sells the articles for public use, the damages which he recovers are the substitute for the license-fees which are his due, or for the profits he would have obtained if he himself had sold the article instead of the vendor. Thus by the satisfaction of his judgment he has already once received his lawful recompense for the release of this particular article from the monopoly, and estopped himself from claiming that the title of the purchaser is void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise explains complexity: when patentee recovers full damages and profits from an infringing manufacturer, users who bought that manufacturer's machines may be protected in their continued use if (and to the extent) the patentee's recovery has been satisfied; if patentee's recovery is limited to damages for past infringement (and not profits/licensing value), future infringement may remain actionable. Cases and commentary: Allis v. Stowell, Perrigo v. Spaulding, Spaulding v. Page, and analysis of when recovery operates as satisfaction giving purchasers a license-like protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale by patentee who constructs and sells a machine conveys the right to use that specific machine to fullest practical extent
rubrics_metrics.description: The sale by a person who has the full right to make, sell, and use such a machine carries with it the right to the use of that machine to the full extent to which it can be used in point of time. ... He conveyed his whole right to it — his whole right to the use of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities (Mitchell v. Hawley; Blanchard v. Whitney) are cited to support that when the patentee himself builds and sells a machine, the purchaser gets the use-rights as if the patent had never claimed that specific sold article — the patentee has 'parted with' his exclusive right in that particular item. This supports the general principle that sale by owner conveys broad use-rights for that specific article.
